opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few different limits worth distinguishing, and they behave pretty differently.

One is the limit on the inputs we've been scaling: compute, data, and money. Training compute for frontier runs has been growing at something like four or five x per year. That's partly hardware getting better, but mostly people spending a lot more. You can't keep that going forever. At some point you're spending a meaningful fraction of GDP, or you hit constraints on fab capacity, power, and the time it takes to build data centers. So naively, by around the end of the decade, the pace of compute scaling has to slow a lot unless AI is already producing enough economic value to justify much larger investment. Data is similar: we're getting through the high-quality human text, and the question is how well synthetic data and RL on verifiable tasks fill that gap.

So one model is that progress slows as we approach those limits. If you haven't reached something like full automation of AI R&D by the time the input scaling runs out, timelines get much longer, because then you're relying on slower algorithmic progress and slower hardware improvement. I think that's an important reason to put a fair amount of probability on things happening either relatively soon or quite a bit later, rather than spreading it evenly.

The other way to think about it is that the relevant limit isn't the inputs but the point where AI itself starts speeding up progress. Once AIs can do much of the work of AI researchers, the bottleneck is less how many smart people work on this and more how much compute you have to run experiments and to run the AIs. Then you have to ask whether you get a feedback loop: better AI makes better algorithms, which give you more effective compute, which gives you better AI. Does that loop speed up or fizzle out?

My view is that it plausibly speeds up, at least for a while. The key quantity is roughly how much harder further algorithmic improvements get as you make progress, compared with how much each improvement boosts your research capacity. If returns to research effort are good enough, you can get progress that is quite fast, maybe years of progress compressed into months. But compute is a real bottleneck. You can have many very smart AI researchers, but if they all need to run experiments on a fixed pool of chips, you get diminishing returns from more cognitive labor alone. How substitutable labor and compute are in AI research is one of the biggest uncertainties, and reasonable people end up in quite different places.

Then eventually you do approach real limits: something like the limits of algorithmic efficiency for a given amount of compute, and physical limits on how fast you can build chips and power plants. I expect the software side could saturate surprisingly quickly in a fast takeoff, after which progress is set more by how fast you can scale physical infrastructure, which could itself be accelerated a lot by AI and robotics, but on a slower timescale.

So the picture I'd give is: fast input scaling now, a crunch around the late 2020s where either automation kicks in or things slow down, and if automation kicks in, a possibly very rapid software-driven phase that eventually becomes bottlenecked by compute and physical stuff. I wouldn't be confident in any specific numbers, but I think it's a mistake to just extrapolate current trends smoothly in either direction.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether progress accelerates or slows as limits approach, but does not identify the timing of that shift as determining how many orders of magnitude of progress occur.

r002.rationale: It notes uncertainty and disagreement about bottlenecks, but does not state that empirical data poorly constrain the many parameters in progress models.

r003.rationale: It does not place progress barely faster than its previous pace at the 25th percentile.

r004.rationale: It describes a possibly rapid phase, but does not place extraordinarily rapid progress around the 75th or 80th percentile.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that there are basically two different regimes you need to model separately, and a lot of the disagreement people have comes from collapsing them together.

The first regime is the one we're in now, where progress is mostly driven by scaling inputs: more compute, more data, better algorithms, more people working on it. And in that regime, I think the right picture is something like a fairly steady exponential, where the effective compute going into frontier systems grows at some rate, and the capabilities you get out are a somewhat predictable function of that. The key question there is just how long the input growth can be sustained. Compute spending can't grow at 3-4x per year forever, you eventually hit limits on how much of the economy you can pour into this, on chip production, on energy. So you'd naively expect the pace to slow down sometime in the early 2030s as those constraints bind.

But the second regime is the one that I think matters more, and it's what happens once AI systems themselves start substantially contributing to AI research. At that point the "inputs" are no longer just human labor and compute, you've got AI labor that can be scaled up by running more copies, and that's a feedback loop that can potentially outpace the physical constraints for a while. If you have systems that are as good as your best researchers, and you can run, say, a million of them at 10x human speed, then the question is whether the returns to that cognitive labor are high enough to drive a very fast period of progress, what people sometimes call a software-only intelligence explosion. My current guess is that it's plausible you get a period of maybe a few years where the rate of algorithmic progress is dramatically faster than today, until you hit diminishing returns on the software side and you're back to being bottlenecked on compute and physical stuff.

So when I say "approaching limits," I'd distinguish between limits on inputs, which are real but can be partially bypassed by automation, and limits on how far capabilities can go at a given compute level, which is more uncertain. I don't think we're close to the second kind. There's a huge gap between what current systems do with a given amount of compute and what, say, a human brain does with its energy budget, so there's clearly a lot of room algorithmically.

The honest answer on the overall picture is that I put substantial probability, maybe 25% or something in that range, on fully automating AI R&D within the next several years, and then a long tail where it takes much longer because the current paradigm runs out of steam before you get there. And modeling that well requires being clear about which of those regimes you're actually making a claim about.

r003.rationale: It does not place progress that is only barely faster than the previous pace at the 25th percentile; its 25% estimate concerns automating AI R&D.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish between progress slowing down because some input becomes harder to scale, and progress slowing down because you’re approaching a limit on how well a task can be done. Those can look pretty different.

For inputs, you might imagine that we keep spending more on compute, but eventually it becomes difficult to build enough chips or supply enough power. That could slow things down, though the effect depends on how much progress comes from better algorithms and more efficient use of the compute we already have.

For task performance, you should expect saturation in some places. If a model is already getting nearly every question on a benchmark right, it can’t improve much on that benchmark. But that doesn’t necessarily tell you much about whether it can do a week-long research project reliably. You can have individual measurements flatten out while economically important capabilities continue improving.

So I’d be pretty hesitant to fit one curve and extrapolate it all the way through. I’d want to ask what mechanism is producing the slowdown, and whether it applies to the capabilities we actually care about. And there’s a potentially important complication, which is that AI could help with AI research. Then the rate of improvement itself depends on how capable the systems are, and you could get acceleration even while some of the underlying inputs are becoming harder to scale.

r001.rationale: The response discusses different causes of slowdown and possible acceleration, but does not identify when progress shifts from acceleration to deceleration relative to limits as determining how many orders of magnitude of progress occur.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss how empirical data constrain parameters in models of AI progress approaching limits.

r003.rationale: It gives no percentile estimate or claim that progress barely faster than its previous pace is a plausible 25th-percentile outcome.

r004.rationale: It gives no percentile estimate placing extraordinarily rapid AI progress around the 75th or 80th percentile.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate a few different things that can look like limits. One is that a particular approach starts giving you diminishing returns. Another is that you run into a constraint on an input, like compute or data. And a third is that you’re approaching the best possible performance on the task itself. Those imply pretty different trajectories.

For example, you could see progress slow down on a benchmark because there’s very little room left to improve, while the systems are still becoming substantially more useful. Or you could have a real slowdown because scaling the existing approach stops working as well, but then further progress depends on finding better algorithms.

So I’d be hesitant to fit one curve and extrapolate it all the way through. I’d want a model of what’s driving the improvement, which constraints become binding, and whether AI itself can help relax those constraints. If AI can substantially accelerate research, then diminishing returns to any one research direction don’t necessarily imply slow overall progress—you might explore alternative directions much faster. But that’s a conditional argument, rather than a reason to assume acceleration continues indefinitely.
